Year 5 English · Reading & Writing

Suri’s WallLucy Estela & Matt Ottley

Analyse how the illustrator builds mood, then write in Suri’s voice using inference.

60 minutes Whole class to independent Transcript printed

Success criteria

What success looks like today

I can identify a theme and support it with words and phrases from the text.
I can explain the illustrator’s choices using evidence.
I can write a diary entry in Suri’s voice that shows her thoughts and feelings.

Themes opener 10 min

Big idea: friendship

Teacher think-aloud When I read this text I keep noticing words connected to friendship: warmth, giggling, cuddled up, heart ached, together. I think friendship is one of the big ideas in this story.
Onto the printed transcript. Girls highlight 10 words or phrases that connect to friendship. Quick share of a few before you model the theme statement.
Modelled theme statement In Suri’s Wall we learn the importance of having friends and feeling included. To begin with, the other children leave Suri out and this makes her feel sad and alone. When Suri starts telling stories the children realise she is special, and they spend more time with her.

Leave the theme statement on the board. It feeds the diary task later, the diary is the same emotional arc seen from the inside.

I do · Model the analysis 12 min

The cold world

Teacher think-aloud Look at the colours first, muted greys and shadows, hardly any light, and that already feels cold and sad. Now the angle, we are looking at Suri from far away, a wide shot, and it makes her tiny in this big empty space. And her body, shoulders turned away, curled in. He is using all of it together to make us feel how alone she is.
SceneWhat we noticeIllustrator choicesHow it makes us feel
Suri alone by the wall Empty courtyard, no toys, Suri small and turned away Muted greys, deep shadows, little light, wide shot, Suri off to the side Cold, lonely, heartbroken
Key question, left on the board: Why did the illustrator choose this? What is he trying to make us feel?

The thinking move · inference

How we work out what isn’t said

Every time we say how a scene makes us feel, we are inferring. The illustrator never writes “Suri is lonely”. We work it out from the clues he leaves, joined to what we already know.

I notice

a clue in the picture or the words

+
I know

something from my own life

=
So I infer

what Suri is thinking or feeling

Worked example · Suri alone by the wall

I notice

Suri is turned away, drawn tiny in a big empty courtyard, painted in cold greys.

I know

when someone makes themselves small and turns away, they often feel left out or sad.

So I infer

Suri feels lonely and wishes someone would notice her, even though the book never says so.

We do · Over the wall 10 min

The world Suri describes

  • What colours has he used here compared to the courtyard? (vivid, warm, light)
  • Does anything feel big or powerful now?
  • Why has he made it look so different?
Make the contrast explicit The world the children actually live in is grey. The world Suri describes is bursting with colour. Why does that contrast matter? What do Suri’s stories give the other children?
Listening for: stories bring colour, hope and escape; Suri has something the others don’t; imagination changes how the grey world feels. Tie it back to the friendship statement on the board.

You do · Timeline, then diary 18 min

Write in Suri’s voice

Choose a moment when Suri changes, then write a diary entry from inside it.

From your inference to a diary line

First infer how Suri feels at your moment. Then don’t tell us the feeling, show it through what she sees, does or remembers.

Telling · avoid

“I felt lonely and left out today.”

Showing · aim for

“I dragged my hand along the cold stones again. Somewhere behind me the others were laughing, but no one called my name.”

Part 1 · 4 min · choose a moment

  1. Scraping her hand along the wall, excluded and alone.
  2. Realising she can see over the wall, taller at last.
  3. Eva taking her hand as she describes what is over the wall.
  4. More children coming to listen, the shared dinner.
  5. Deciding to keep telling stories despite the guard’s warning.

Part 2 · 14 min · write the entry

Diary scaffold

  • First person (“I”), past tense.
  • Start with where she is and what just happened.
  • Show how she feels through details, don’t just name the feeling.
  • End with what has changed for her.

Sentence starters

  • Today by the wall I…
  • I never thought anyone would…
  • When Eva took my hand I felt…

Plenary 10 min

Share and infer

Pairs swap diary entries. Each partner finds one inference about Suri’s feelings that was not stated directly in the text, and reads it out.

Use the frame:

I think Suri felt   because the writer showed  , even though they never said it.

Quick class share: which moment did most people choose, and why that one?

Exit slip

The illustrator chose   to show   because  .
